Most platforms force a single runtime. Clawfleet runs both — agencies route cost-sensitive workloads to Hermes, integration- heavy ones to OpenClaw, and bill them through one dashboard.

OpenClaw

Ecosystem-first

Pick OpenClaw when your workload needs the ClawHub catalog — browser automation, CRM connectors, multi-step orchestration, or long-context reasoning.

  • 11,000+ verified skills (after vetting)
  • Multi-step planner + browser tooling
  • Long-context tasks, content workflows

Hermes

Cost-first

Pick Hermes when you run high volumes of short, templated prompts — daily briefs, reporting, inbox triage, or LLM querying — and want the cost curve to stay flat.

  • ~3-5x cheaper per call on low-complexity prompts
  • Sub-second cold start on warm pods
  • Deterministic outputs for templated work

The Reality

Self-Hosting an AI Agent Is a Nightmare

OpenClaw and Hermes are both incredible software. But getting either running on your own server? That's where the dream dies for 95% of users.

r/selfhosted

"I spent 3 hours and still can't get Docker working."

Self-hosting an AI agent — OpenClaw, Hermes, or anything else — means a VPS, SSH, Node.js, Docker, and an interactive setup wizard. Most people quit before sending their first message.

Discord community

"My bot went down at 3 AM and nobody told me."

Self-hosted agents crash silently. Docker runs out of memory. Node throws exceptions. Without monitoring, your assistant dies and you find out days later.

Security research, Jan 2026

"900+ agent gateways are exposed without auth."

Misconfigured Docker ports and missing auth tokens mean your API keys and conversations are visible to anyone with a search engine. Same risk on every runtime if you cut corners.

User interviews

"I'm spending $47/week on AI and have no idea where it goes."

Self-hosted agents ship with zero cost visibility. Skills loop, tokens burn, and you only discover the damage when the credit card bill arrives.
